title: The Holy Hesychast
subtitle: The Hagioritic Tome of 1340, the Apolytikia, and a guided summary of the Triads
source: St. Gregory Palamas's own writings and the Hagioritic Tome have no public-domain English that we have found, so this page tells their teaching in our words, marked as ours, and gives no quotation as theirs. The apolytikion is in the public-domain English of The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom: The Greek Text with a Rendering in English (London: Williams & Norgate, 1914); the kontakion is in our English, no public-domain translation of it having been found. The closing prayer was written for Purify. By the editors of Purify.

sections.title: On St. Gregory and the hesychast controversy
sections.framing: St. Gregory Palamas's principal writings, the nine treatises of the Triads in Defense of the Holy Hesychasts (1338-1341), the One Hundred and Fifty Chapters, the great Synodal Tomos of 1351, and his many homilies, are mostly preserved in good critical Greek editions but in modern English translations that remain under copyright. The public-domain English we can serve in full is the much shorter Hagioritic Tome of 1340, the brief Athonite confession Gregory co-drafted with the elders of the Holy Mountain in support of the hesychast practice; this is given verbatim in section 3 below. For the rest, this work gives a guided summary of the central teaching, written in the project's own voice with direct quotations clearly marked, and the standard liturgical hymns of his two feasts in their PD English form.
paragraphs: The reader who wishes to read the Triads or the Capita 150 in full will need to seek out the modern translations (Meyendorff for the Triads, Sinkewicz for the Capita), which the Church owes a real debt to and which are well worth their cost. What follows is an honest introduction to the saint's teaching, given as the project can give it from the public domain.

sections.title: Apolytikion of St. Gregory Palamas (Tone 8)
sections.framing: Sung on the Second Sunday of Great Lent and on November 14, the two days the Church keeps his memory.
paragraphs: O Gregory, Wonder-worker, Torch-bearer of Orthodoxy, and support and teacher of the Church, the ornament of the Cloister, the unconquerable champion of Theologians, the boast of Thessalonica, and the preacher of grace, supplicate ever for the salvation of our souls.
sections.citation: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom: The Greek Text with a Rendering in English (London, 1914), p. 86, the Dismissal Hymn of the Second Sunday of the Fast

sections.title: The Hagioritic Tome (1340), in our words
sections.framing: Drafted by Gregory and signed by the elders of the Holy Mountain in 1340 as the Athonite community's formal answer to the philosophical attacks of Barlaam the Calabrian. It is the briefest and most direct of all the Palamite documents: a short confession of what the hesychasts have received in the tradition of the Mountain and will not surrender to the philosophers' analysis.
paragraphs: The elders of the Holy Mountain set down in the Tome what they had received from their fathers in the monastic life: that the light which shone from the Lord's body on Tabor, and which the saints will see in the age to come, is not a created symbol but the uncreated and deifying grace of God, the glory of the divine nature, His own and not another's.

They confess that those who in this life have been made worthy of this grace, by keeping the commandments and by long prayer of the heart, see not something created in God's place but the energy and glory of God Himself, as the disciples saw it on the mountain; and that to deny this is to deny the deification of man and to make the grace of the Holy Spirit a created thing.

They hold, with the Fathers, that God is not shared in His essence and is truly shared in His energies, and they declare that any teaching to the contrary, however learned, is foreign to the Apostles, the Fathers and the Church, and that they will not receive it.
notes: The Hagioritic Tome was received by the local Constantinopolitan synod of 1341 and incorporated into the later Synodal Tomos of 1351, the formal Palamite definition placed in the Synodikon of Orthodoxy and read aloud on the Sunday of Orthodoxy.
No public-domain English of the Tome has been found. This is a summary in our words, not a translation.

sections.title: The teaching of the Triads (a guided summary in the project's voice)
sections.framing: The Triads in Defense of the Holy Hesychasts (1338-1341) are nine treatises in three sets of three. The first Triad answers Barlaam on the legitimacy of the hesychast bodily prayer; the second on whether the saints' experience of God is a created illumination; the third on the distinction between God's essence and His energies. The summary below is the project's own, with verbatim quotations from the Tomos of 1351 (which preserves the Triads' substance) clearly marked as such.
paragraphs: Barlaam's attack came in three waves. He attacked the hesychasts' bodily prayer (the joining of the Jesus Prayer to the breath, the practice of looking inward toward the heart) as a vulgar materialism. He attacked their claim that pure-hearted ascetics could behold an uncreated divine light as a confusion between God's essence and a created symbol. And he attacked their teaching that God can be truly known in something other than the bare logical concept of His existence as a denial of the apophatic tradition of Pseudo-Dionysius. Gregory answered each wave in turn.

On the bodily prayer: man is not a soul alone but a soul-and-body unity. The prayer that sanctifies the man cannot be a prayer of the mind alone, leaving the body untouched; it must work through the breath, the heart, the whole person. The hesychast posture (the bowed head, the gaze toward the heart, the breath joined to the Name) is the body's participation in the prayer of the soul, and is no more materialistic than the kneeling at the Eucharist or the kissing of the icon. Christ took a body; the Spirit comes to bodies; the saints are saved in body and in soul together.

On the uncreated light: what the three disciples saw on Tabor was not a created symbol of God but the divine glory itself, the same that filled the tabernacle of Moses and that will fill the saints at the age to come. The Synodal Tomos of 1351 confesses the same: the light is not a creature but uncreated, the very glory of the divine nature. The saints who in this life are granted to see it, see God Himself, not a representation of God.

On the essence and the energies: the divine essence is unknowable and incommunicable to any creature; if it were communicable, the creature would become identical with God by nature, which is impossible. But the divine energies, the operations, the grace, the glory, are God Himself in His self-communication, truly God and yet truly communicable. The saints partake of God by the energies, not by the essence; they are deified, made gods by grace and not by nature. The distinction is not a division in God (God is one and simple) but a distinction between what God is in Himself and what God is toward us in His self-revelation.

Palamas put it succinctly in the formula the Tomos of 1351 takes from the Triads: the illumination, or divine and deifying grace, is not the essence but the energy of God. To deny the distinction is either to make God essentially knowable (so denying the apophatic tradition and reducing God to a concept) or to make the saints' experience of God a created thing (so denying the deification the Fathers have preached from the beginning). The Eastern Orthodox Church has held the Palamite distinction as the grammar of her mystical theology ever since.

sections.title: On the Jesus Prayer
sections.framing: A summary in our words of the first Triad's defense of the hesychast practice.
paragraphs: The Jesus Prayer is not a technique but a return to the heart. The hesychast tradition received it from the apostolic preaching: that the Lord is named in the breath and the heart together, that the mind is gathered out of its scattering and led down to the place where the breath enters and the love of God is kindled, that the Name is repeated quietly enough to be heard within and persistently enough to remain when speech has ceased.

Palamas defended the bodily side of the prayer (the gaze toward the heart, the joining of the prayer to the breath) against Barlaam's charge of vulgarity: the body too is sanctified, the body too will be raised in glory, and the body shares already, in this life, in the grace of the Spirit, when it is brought into the prayer of the heart.

The prayer the hesychasts offer is short and unceasing: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner. It is not the Lord's Prayer (which has its own place in the Liturgy and in the rule of the cell); it is not a substitute for the offices of the Church; it is the breath-prayer of the watchful heart, taught by the desert Fathers and given new precision by the Athonites of the fourteenth century, that the praying Christian may keep the Name on his lips and in his mind as continually as he keeps his breath.

sections.title: Kontakion of St. Gregory (Tone 8)
paragraphs: Holy and divine instrument of wisdom, harmonious trumpet of theology, we sing your praises with one voice, O divinely inspired Gregory. As a mind that stood before the Original Mind, direct our minds to Him, O Father, that we may cry to you: Rejoice, herald of grace.
sections.citation: Our English, not a public-domain translation

sections.title: A prayer to St. Gregory, written for Purify
paragraphs: O Holy Father Gregory, intercede with Christ our God that the light you saw on Tabor and confessed against the philosophers may shine in our hearts, that we may be granted, with you and with all the saints, the prayer of the heart and the grace of the deifying energies, now and unto the ages of ages. Amen.
